name: Valerian root
lead: Valerian is a perennial plant (Valeriana officinalis) native to Europe and southwestern Asia whose dried root is a traditional herbal remedy and a common over-the-counter supplement, mainly for sleep and nervous tension [1]. In looksmaxxing and recovery communities it appears in bedtime and anxiety-calming routines.

Research on its effect on sleep is mixed. Wikipedia summarizes a 2010 meta-analysis and a 2006 systematic review as suggesting possible benefit, while a 2015 systematic review and a 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline described effectiveness as weak or inconclusive; a 2020 meta-analysis concluded it may be safe and effective and suggested inconsistent results could reflect variable extract quality [1][2]. A 2006 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for anxiety disorders [1].
infobox: EMA recognizes a dry root extract as a well-established herbal medicine; US: generally recognized as safe at common doses

paras: The root contains a volatile oil with sesquiterpenes such as valerenic acid, along with iridoids (valepotriates), alkaloids and flavonoids [1]. Laboratory work found a binding site on GABA-A receptors for valerenic acid and valerenol, where they enhanced the response to GABA [3]. Rat experiments reported anxiolytic behavior with root extracts [4], and zebrafish studies reported delayed seizure onset [5]. These are preclinical findings.

A 1982 study of 128 people comparing an aqueous valerian extract with placebo and a commercial preparation reported a significant decrease in subjectively rated sleep latency [6]. Other early human studies include a 1985 paper on valerian and human sleep [7] and a 1989 double-blind study [8]. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis examined valerian for sleep problems and related disorders [9]. Registered trials have tested valerian in older adults, people with Parkinson's disease, menopausal women, combinations with lavender or poppy extracts, and dental anxiety [10][11][12][13][14].

Headache and diarrhea occurred in clinical studies, and use is discouraged in pregnancy; as it can depress the central nervous system, it should not be combined with alcohol, benzodiazepines or other sedatives [1]. A 1998 JAMA report described cardiac complications and delirium associated with valerian withdrawal [15]. Product concentration and contaminants vary because supplements are loosely regulated [1]. A US drug label for a valerian, passionflower and magnesium carbonate product advises pregnant or nursing people to seek professional advice [16].
Valerian has been used since ancient Greece and Rome; Hippocrates described its properties and Galen prescribed it for insomnia [1].

card.summary: A classic herbal sleep aid with mixed trial results and some withdrawal and sedative-interaction cautions.
card.note: Additive with alcohol and sedatives; avoid in pregnancy per sources.

quick.overview:
Valerian root is an old European herbal remedy sold for sleep and nervous tension. It shows up in sleep stacks in recovery and appearance communities.

Reviews disagree: some find modest sleep benefits, others call evidence weak or inconclusive.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory work suggests valerenic acid enhances GABA-A receptor activity, similar in general direction to calming drugs, though the in-human relevance is unproven.
quick.risks: Reported effects include headache and diarrhea; it can add to the sedation of alcohol and other sedatives, and pregnancy use is discouraged. A 1998 report described delirium and cardiac complications on withdrawal.
